report.summary: Section 15 imposes costly manual checks and a sequential amendment log that will become a maintenance bottleneck; no cheaper alternative is offered for the atomicity guarantee.
risks: 15.1 | medium | 'Ordinary tasks must not edit the plan...' – adds runtime enforcement cost for every task; cheaper: rely on file permissions and code review without runtime checks.
15.2 | medium | Steps 1-7 are a rigid sequential protocol; cheaper: automate steps 3-7 with a script that checks prerequisites.
15.3 | high | 'Increment the plan revision monotonically' – requires a global counter; cheaper: use commit hash or timestamp as revision.
15.4 | medium | 'Append exactly one accepted record to ...amendments.jsonl' – sequential log becomes a bottleneck under concurrent amendments; cheaper: use a distributed log or allow batch records.
15.5 | medium | 'Update the plan, ledger, derived controls, and tests atomically' – no atomicity mechanism defined; cheaper: rely on versioned files and idempotent updates.
15.6 | high | 'Run policy verification and the relevant fault-injection suite' – expensive per amendment; cheaper: run only on merge to main.
15.7 | low | 'The environment token only unlocks the protected files for that process' – adds complexity; cheaper: use standard access control.
15.8 | low | 'It does not waive owner approval...' – duplicates existing checks; cheaper: rely on a single approval gate.
15.9 | low | 'Rollback is a new amendment, never a history rewrite' – forces sequential rollbacks; cheaper: allow revert commits.
todos: Replace manual amendment steps with a script that automates token validation, revision increment, log append, and atomic file update.
Replace monotonic revision counter with a commit hash or timestamp to avoid global state.
Allow batch amendment records to reduce log contention.
Move policy and fault-injection runs to integration pipeline instead of per-amendment requirement.
Remove redundant 'does not waive' clause; combine owner approval with token enforcement.

claims.claim: Ordinary tasks must not edit the plan, amendment chain, active instructions, or guards.
claims.why: This rule adds runtime enforcement cost for every ordinary task. A cheaper alternative is to rely on file permissions and code review without runtime checks.

claims.claim: To amend: 1. Propose the exact diff, reason, alternatives, affected invariants/priors, migration, rollback, evidence, and owner. 2. Obtain explicit repository-owner approval. 3. Start the amendment session with DAEDALUS_IRON_PLAN_AMENDMENT=<current full plan sha256>. 4. Increment the plan revision monotonically. 5. Append exactly one accepted record to docs/IKARUS_ARIADNE_MASTER_PLAN.amendments.jsonl. It records base/result SHA-256, previous-record hash, approval reference, scope, and evidence. 6. Update the plan, ledger, derived controls, and tests atomically. 7. Run policy verification and the relevant fault-injection suite.
claims.why: The seven-step protocol is rigid and manual, forcing high engineering effort per amendment. Many steps (3-7) can be automated with a script that checks prerequisites, reducing cost without sacrificing guarantees.

claims.claim: The environment token only unlocks the protected files for that process.
claims.why: Token-based access is a standard pattern; cost is moderate but acceptable. No cheaper alternative that provides equivalent isolation.

claims.claim: It does not waive owner approval, the amendment record, review, or evidence.
claims.why: This clause duplicates the requirements already stated in step 2. A cheaper alternative is to combine owner approval with token enforcement, removing redundancy.

claims.claim: Rollback is a new amendment, never a history rewrite.
claims.why: Forcing rollbacks as new amendments creates sequential dependencies and extra log entries. A cheaper alternative is to allow revert commits that directly undo changes, which is simpler and faster.
Monotonic increment requires a global counter, which is a scalability bottleneck and adds coordination cost. A cheaper alternative is to use the commit hash or a timestamp as the revision identifier.

claims.claim: Append exactly one accepted record to docs/IKARUS_ARIADNE_MASTER_PLAN.amendments.jsonl.
claims.why: A single JSONL file forces sequential writes, creating a bottleneck under concurrent amendments. A cheaper alternative is to use a distributed log (e.g., append to separate files per amendment) or allow batch records.

claims.claim: Update the plan, ledger, derived controls, and tests atomically.
claims.why: Atomic update across multiple files is expensive and error-prone without a transaction system. A cheaper alternative is to rely on versioned files and idempotent update scripts that can be retried.

claims.claim: Run policy verification and the relevant fault-injection suite.
claims.why: Running these suites per amendment is costly in time and resources. A cheaper alternative is to run them only on merge to main, relying on pre-commit checks for basic validation.
